subject: chemistry
title: Mixtures vs Compounds
welcome_lead: Stir, shake or pour: when substances are not chemically joined, they form a mixture.
meta_desc: Compare mixtures and compounds in this KS3 chemistry adventure on pure substances and impure substances.
final_note: You can now spot the difference between a mixture and a compound.

concepts.def: Two or more substances not chemically joined together.
A mixture where a solid dissolves into a liquid.
A mixture of metals, like brass (copper and zinc).
A mixture of gases including nitrogen and oxygen.
Mixtures can be split by physical means.
Mixtures can have any ratio of substances.

walkthroughs.body_html:
A mixture contains two or more substances that are not chemically joined. Each substance keeps its own properties.

Mixtures can be separated using physical methods like filtering, evaporating or distilling.

In a compound, atoms are bonded in fixed ratios. In a mixture, the ratio can vary.

A compound has new properties. A mixture keeps the old properties of its parts.

Bonded = compound. Just mixed = mixture.

Salty seawater, fizzy drinks, the air you breathe and metal alloys like brass are all mixtures.

Pure water (H₂O) is a compound; tap water is a mixture of water and dissolved minerals.

mcqs.q: For a process to be spontaneous, what must happen to the total entropy of the universe?
options: The entropy of the system must increase for the process to be spontaneous.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
It must increase (ΔS_total > 0) — the system's entropy alone can decrease as long as the surroundings' entropy increases more.
The entropy of the surroundings must stay constant for the process to be spontaneous.

mcqs.q: Why do tertiary halogenoalkanes typically react via SN1 rather than SN2?
options: The tertiary carbocation intermediate is stabilised by three alkyl groups (positive inductive effect), making the SN1 pathway favourable.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN1 because they are more reactive in every way.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene undergo electrophilic SUBSTITUTION but alkenes undergo electrophilic ADDITION?
options: Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
Benzene reacts the same way as alkenes — by addition across one of its double bonds.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.
Substitution preserves benzene's stable delocalised pi system; addition would destroy aromaticity at a large energetic cost.
